opus-5.5.text:
I think these are actually two quite different ideas, even though both involve vision.

When we talk about robots learning from YouTube videos, the point is really about the **data source**. Robot data is extremely expensive. Every trajectory needs a physical robot, a human operator doing teleoperation, and lots of time and money. Meanwhile, the internet holds an enormous number of videos of humans cooking, folding clothes, fixing things. So the question is whether we can extract useful knowledge from that data: what the task is, what the steps are, what a successful outcome looks like, and roughly how objects should move. It's a way of getting semantic and task-level understanding, maybe some motion priors, without collecting everything on a robot.

But a video alone doesn't give you everything. It has no action labels. You see a human hand, not a robot gripper, so there's an embodiment gap. And critically, you don't see forces: how hard to grip, how much friction there is, what happens on contact. So learning from video is a powerful way to bootstrap, but you still need robot data, or simulation, or reinforcement learning, to close the gap to actual physical execution.

"Solving all problems entirely through vision" is a claim about the **sensing modality**, whether a camera is enough as the robot's only input. For many tasks, vision gets you surprisingly far, and recent progress in vision-language-action models shows that. But for contact-rich manipulation, like inserting a plug, handling something fragile, or doing something in the dark or under occlusion, vision alone is very hard. Humans rely heavily on touch and proprioception for those. Try tying your shoes with numb fingers; your eyes don't save you.

So, in short: learning from YouTube is about where knowledge comes from, while vision-only is about what the robot perceives at runtime. You can do the first without believing the second. My own view is that internet video will be a huge part of how robots acquire common sense about the world, but for robots to be truly dexterous and reliable, we'll likely need richer sensing, especially touch, alongside vision.

r001.rationale: It describes extracting task knowledge from internet videos without collecting everything on a robot, while noting that additional data may be needed for physical execution.

r002.rationale: It contrasts costly robot data collection with the enormous number of available internet videos, conveying video data’s scalability.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes video learning as a knowledge source from vision-only as the robot’s runtime sensing modality.

fable-5.1.text:
Those are actually two very different things, and I think people conflate them a lot.

Learning from YouTube is really a question of where the data comes from. The robot, or more precisely the model behind it, is watching humans do things, and it tries to extract something useful out of that: how a hand approaches a cup, what sequence of steps it takes to fold a shirt, what the goal state looks like. The nice thing is that the internet has an enormous amount of this. You could never collect that much data with real robots. The hard part is the gap: the video has a human body, not a robot body, there is no action label telling you what torques were applied, and the camera viewpoint is arbitrary. So you learn a kind of high-level prior, an understanding of tasks and intentions, and then you still have to ground that in the robot's own embodiment, usually through some amount of real robot data or simulation.

Solving everything through vision is a different claim. That is about what sensor the robot uses at deployment time. It says the robot only looks at the world through cameras and maps pixels directly to actions, with no tactile sensing, no force sensors, maybe not even precise proprioception. That is appealing because cameras are cheap and vision models are very strong now. But vision alone has real limits. If you grasp something slippery, or you are inserting a connector, the information you need is in contact forces, and you cannot see that. Occlusion is another problem, your own gripper blocks the camera at exactly the moment that matters.

So one is about the training signal, the other is about the sensing modality. You can learn from YouTube and still use touch at run time, and you can be purely vision-based without ever having watched a human video. In my own work I tend to think of internet video as a way to teach the robot what to do, and I think the robot still needs its own experience, with whatever sensors are useful, to learn how to do it.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from YouTube videos, but does not state that this can happen without teleoperation; it says the learned knowledge still needs grounding through robot data or simulation.

r002.rationale: It says the internet contains an enormous amount of video data and that robots could never collect as much data themselves, directly linking video’s value to scale.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes video as a training signal from vision-only sensing at deployment, and says the two approaches can occur independently.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two different questions. Learning from YouTube is about where the training data comes from. Solving tasks entirely through vision is about what information the robot uses to act.

A video can show a robot what a task looks like—the steps involved, how objects move, and what success looks like. But it doesn’t directly tell the robot what forces to apply or how to move its own joints. So there’s still a gap between watching someone do something and being able to do it yourself.

And learning from video doesn’t mean the robot has to rely only on cameras when it performs the task. It could also use touch, force sensing, and information about its joint positions. For example, a video might show you how to insert a plug, but feeling the contact can help you make the small adjustments needed to actually insert it. So learning from video and using multiple senses are quite compatible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from YouTube videos but does not state that this can happen without teleoperation.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute video data’s value to scalability.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes video as a source of training data from using only vision to act, and notes that robots can use touch, force, and joint-position information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two different questions. Learning from YouTube videos is about where the training data comes from. Solving tasks through vision is about what information the robot uses when it acts.

A video can show a robot what a task looks like—how someone opens a drawer, for example—but it doesn’t directly provide the forces or motor commands needed to do it. The robot still has to connect what it sees to its own actions, through interaction and practice.

And learning from video doesn’t mean the robot should use only cameras. It can also use joint positions, force sensing, or touch. Vision gives you a lot of information, but when you’re making contact with the world, those other signals can be very useful.
